title: Room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk polycrystalline structural ceramics

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a refractory structural ceramic that can undergo permanent stretching at room temperature while remaining a coherent bulk polycrystalline solid. In a specimen representative of a structural application, it would exhibit tensile yielding, measurable uniform plastic elongation, and strain hardening: after yielding, additional deformation would require increasing stress. The intended deformation mechanism is dislocation motion, in which defects move through the crystal lattice and allow it to change shape.

Scope synthesis: the target concerns high-melting oxides, nitrides, or carbides composed of many grains, rather than only individual crystals or microscopic specimens. The breakthrough would establish sustained tensile plastic flow across interacting grains at a useful specimen scale. Local deformation under an indenter, single-crystal compression, and tensile deformation of a soft ceramic such as silver chloride demonstrate relevant phenomena but do not establish this narrower refractory structural capability.

significance.text: Conventional structural ceramics commonly fail through flaw-driven crack propagation before developing appreciable tensile plasticity. Establishing room-temperature tensile yielding and hardening in a bulk refractory polycrystal would therefore introduce a major new mechanical behavior for the demonstrated ceramic family. Its significance would lie in controlled permanent deformation under tension, rather than merely higher strength before sudden fracture.

Engineering synthesis: designers could incorporate a measured yield strength and plastic response alongside fracture and statistical reliability limits. Plastic forming could become possible within the demonstrated strain, geometry, and loading range, potentially reducing dependence on machining sintered blanks. A successful tensile coupon would establish the underlying capability; extensive forming, complex components, and economical production would require further development.

Tensile ductility would not automatically establish damage tolerance or high fracture toughness. The 2025 review describes ceramics, including MgO and NaCl, that exhibit substantial room-temperature dislocation plasticity without demonstrated effective crack-tip blunting. Whether the proposed refractory polycrystal could resist crack initiation or slow crack growth would require separate fracture measurements. Improved damage tolerance is a possible downstream outcome, consistent with the conditional outlook of the September 2026 review abstract, rather than an assured consequence of yielding.

Engineering synthesis: metal-like tensile flow in a ceramic would not make it a general replacement for metals or superalloys. Such substitution would also depend on environmental resistance, service-temperature strength and deformation, durability, and manufacturing cost. Likewise, combining tensile ductility with exceptionally high hardness would be an additional materials target. This concept adopts neither a greater-than-10% elongation requirement nor a 30 GPa hardness floor; the supplied evidence does not establish the feasibility or necessity of that combination.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is compatible, dislocation-mediated tensile plastic deformation across many grains in a bulk refractory ceramic at room temperature, before fracture terminates the process. Most ceramics have too few independent active slip systems at room temperature to satisfy the classical five-system criterion for arbitrary compatible plastic shape change by slip. Neighboring grains can consequently struggle to accommodate one another's deformation, and slip incompatibility or dislocation pileups can initiate grain-boundary cracks. This is a documented cracking risk, not a claim that every grain must crack immediately when another grain shears.

The five-system criterion concerns general deformation accommodated by crystallographic slip; it is not a universal requirement for every possible plastic mechanism. Nevertheless, a successful route must explain how the polycrystal accommodates strain throughout the specimen. Dislocation mobility, the availability and activation of dislocation sources, and competition between plastic flow and fracture remain essential barriers even where some slip is possible.

Mechanically seeding dislocations addresses the difficulty of initiating plasticity in crystals with insufficient operative sources. The research reports an estimate that homogeneous dislocation nucleation can require stresses roughly one to two orders of magnitude above the actual fracture strength of most ceramics. That estimate comes from the prior publisher-text extract described in the research and should be treated as an explanatory estimate, not a universal measured ratio for every ceramic. Providing dislocations still does not, by itself, resolve compatible deformation across grain boundaries or stable tensile flow at component scale.

current_state.text: The review Room-temperature dislocation plasticity in ceramics: Methods, materials, and mechanisms was submitted as a preprint on 6 April 2025 and, according to the supplied research, first published in the Journal of the American Ceramic Society on 16 April 2025. Its 44-compound toolbox reports room-temperature dislocation-based plastic deformation in single crystals for every listed compound. That is substantial evidence that ceramic dislocations can move at room temperature, but it is not a set of 44 bulk polycrystalline tensile demonstrations. The review also explains that plasticity observed by nanoindentation need not extend to bulk specimens and identifies bulk tensile testing as the decisive validation goal.

The same review acknowledges polycrystalline tensile deformation in AgCl. Consequently, it would be incorrect to describe room-temperature polycrystalline tensile deformation as wholly unknown across all ceramics. AgCl falls outside this concept's refractory structural scope, so its existence neither completes nor invalidates the proposed innovation.

Harvesting room-temperature plasticity in ceramics by mechanically seeded dislocations appeared in Materials Today 82 (2025), pages 81–91, with an associated arXiv preprint. The supplied review of its full text reports approximately 32% plastic strain without fracture in submicrometer single-crystal SrTiO3 compression and approximately 25% at microscale. These are reported experimental compression results, not projections, and they demonstrate substantial plasticity in the tested model system. They do not demonstrate bulk polycrystalline tensile ductility.

The seeded-dislocation paper's main text assigns the approximately 32% result to submicrometer compression, while its supplementary table inconsistently places a greater-than-32% value in a micropillar row. The scale assignment is therefore not fully consistent within the retained text; the main-text distinction between approximately 32% at submicrometer scale and approximately 25% at microscale is preserved here. The supplied evidence review assessed extracted text, including methods and supplementary material, but did not visually inspect figures or movies. This limits independent assessment of the visual evidence and does not establish that the reported strains are false.

Rethinking brittleness in ceramics: The emergence of room-temperature plasticity, published in the Journal of Advanced Ceramics on 4 September 2026, states in its abstract that reliable and scalable bulk ceramic plasticity remains challenging. Only the article's abstract and identifying information were available in the retained copy; the full review body was absent despite the HTML extraction being untruncated. The abstract supports an ongoing broad scalability challenge, but cannot establish the absence of every possible demonstration meeting this concept's exact refractory, polycrystalline, tensile requirements.

Evidence synthesis: the supplied sources establish substantial room-temperature ceramic dislocation plasticity and motivate the bulk refractory polycrystalline tensile target. They do not supply a demonstration meeting the complete target. Because the freshness search record is empty and the latest retained source is a September 2026 abstract, they also do not establish an exhaustive absence of qualifying results through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: test a polycrystalline refractory oxide, nitride, or carbide coupon in tension at room temperature, using a cross-section and grain structure representative of a specified structural application. It should show a distinct tensile yield, measurable uniform plastic elongation, and strain hardening while remaining a coherent specimen. Confirm that dislocation motion carries the plastic deformation. The literature's emphasis on bulk tensile validation motivates this proposal, but does not make all of these requirements a published consensus criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Bulk room-temperature tensile plasticity with strain hardening from dislocation motion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting and reproducibility requirements: disclose composition, processing, specimen and gauge dimensions, grain-size distribution, temperature, loading rate, and strain-measurement method. Separate permanent plastic strain from elastic strain, machine compliance, grip motion, and strain produced by cracking. Combine mechanical measurements with microstructural evidence of dislocation activity and the distribution of damage. Report repeatability across specimens and processing batches; independent reproduction would strengthen the demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Report methods, verified plastic strain, and repeatability across processing batches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: document the uniform plastic strain range, strength, hardening behavior, failure mode, and sensitivity to specimen size and microstructure. No numerical elongation threshold or hardness floor is imposed. Single-crystal compression, indentation toughness, micropillar deformation, or soft-halide tension alone would not meet the specified scope. Finite successful tests would establish the demonstrated range of materials and conditions, not universal ductility across ceramics, geometries, or loading histories.
completion_criteria.label: Document tensile plasticity limits across specimen sizes and microstructures

completion_criteria.text: Proposed follow-on qualification: claims of damage tolerance should require separate crack-growth and fracture-resistance measurements. Claims about component use, extensive forming, or superalloy replacement should additionally be tested under the relevant environmental, thermal, manufacturing, and service conditions. These are application qualifications beyond demonstrating the central tensile-plasticity capability.
completion_criteria.label: Qualify damage-tolerance and application claims through separate relevant testing

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRM-02, Load-bearing ceramics that survive long service in air above the silica limit, addresses environmental and high-temperature service capability. CRM-01 addresses room-temperature tensile deformation. Combining the two could broaden structural applications, but success in either does not establish the other. CRM-07, A low-activation structural ceramic that keeps its heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation, similarly targets a distinct service constraint: irradiation tolerance and retained heat transport.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-08, Stoichiometric silicon-carbide fiber and composites at general industrial cost, concerns an affordable fiber and composite platform. It could complement ductile ceramic development through structural design and cost reduction, but composite performance would not by itself demonstrate dislocation-mediated tensile ductility in a bulk polycrystalline ceramic. CRM-11, Net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics, and CRM-04, Densification of arbitrary structural ceramics without a high-temperature furnace cycle, address shaping and consolidation. They could improve production of candidate materials without establishing their tensile plasticity.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-12, Large transparent ceramics whose failure stress approaches theoretical strength, pursues high failure stress through control of strength-limiting defects; such a material could remain brittle. CRM-01 instead pursues permanent tensile deformation before fracture. Flaw reduction and ductility can be complementary, but neither mechanism substitutes for demonstrating the other. CRM-05, Repeated, in-service restoration of strength after critical cracks, concerns recovery after damage, whereas CRM-01 concerns deformation during loading. Ductility does not establish crack healing.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-03's ceramic electrolyte, CRM-06's useful room-temperature superconducting ceramic conductor, CRM-09's olefin–paraffin separation membranes, and CRM-10's sunlight-to-fuel oxide ceramic target different functional properties. Mechanical deformability could eventually matter to their manufacture or durability, but the supplied material establishes no direct dependence on CRM-01 and no basis for merging these entries.

change_log.change: Preserved CRM-01's identity and refractory bulk polycrystalline tensile scope while explaining yielding, uniform plastic elongation, and strain hardening.
change_log.reason: The concept remains substantive despite corrections to individual causal or evidentiary assertions.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim about most crystals lacking five slip systems with the ceramic-specific room-temperature barrier, and qualified grain-boundary cracking as a risk.
change_log.reason: The evidence concerns most ceramics at room temperature and does not establish inevitable immediate cracking or a universal requirement covering every deformation mechanism.

change_log.change: Changed damage tolerance from a direct consequence to a separately testable potential outcome, and retained fracture limits alongside yield strength.
change_log.reason: The supplied review documents dislocation plasticity without effective crack-tip blunting in some ceramics.

change_log.change: Expanded the seeded-dislocation result into approximately 32% submicrometer and approximately 25% microscale single-crystal compression, with the supplementary-table inconsistency retained.
change_log.reason: The unqualified beyond-30% statement concealed loading and scale restrictions relevant to the proposed breakthrough.

change_log.change: Distinguished the full-text 2025 evidence, the abstract-only September 2026 review, and the lack of exhaustive freshness coverage.
change_log.reason: The sources support dated achievements and continuing challenges without proving the exact target absent through November 2026.

change_log.change: Retained the nucleation-stress estimate with its prior-extract provenance and limited generality.
change_log.reason: It adds useful mechanistic detail from the research, but the supplied review does not independently resolve the estimate's scope.

change_log.change: Made completion an explicit proposal and added application-defined dimensions, artifact controls, repeatability, and bounded interpretation.
change_log.reason: These make the demonstration reviewable without inventing an established standard or numerical performance threshold.

change_log.change: Removed unsupported historical and comparative hardness assertions while retaining the decision not to impose 10% elongation or 30 GPa hardness requirements.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not substantiate the historical attribution, hardness comparison, or feasibility of the combined target.

change_log.change: Explained numbered relationships using the supplied concept roster, including complementary manufacturing, service, flaw-control, and healing targets.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies titles unavailable to the earlier reviewer; it supports bounded conceptual comparisons while leaving detailed technical interfaces unverified.

unresolved_issues: Whether a qualifying refractory bulk polycrystalline tensile demonstration existed by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; the supplied freshness search record is empty.

The seeded-dislocation paper's main text and supplementary table assign the greater-than-32% strain result inconsistently by specimen scale. Figures and movies were not visually assessed in the supplied review.
The full body of the September 2026 review was unavailable in the retained copy, limiting interpretation beyond its abstract.

Application-specific specimen dimensions, grain-size ranges, reproducibility expectations, and acceptable measurement uncertainty remain to be defined before applying the proposed completion criteria.
The route to compatible intergranular tensile flow, and its relationship to fracture toughness and useful forming strain, remains unresolved for the target refractory ceramic family.

The one-to-two-orders-of-magnitude nucleation-stress estimate is retained with qualification from the research's prior publisher-text extract; its quantitative applicability to particular candidate materials remains unverified.

The earlier recommendation to remove numbered concept relationships was not adopted in full because the supplied roster now provides their titles. The relationships are explicitly roster-based synthesis; detailed definitions and technical dependencies remain unavailable.

brief.title: Structural ceramics that stretch at room temperature
possible: Ceramic parts could stretch permanently under a pulling force at room temperature while staying intact. The target is a heat-resistant ceramic made of many crystal grains, at a size relevant to structural use. Moving defects in the crystals, called dislocations, would let it change shape.

Designers could work with a ceramic that starts to stretch permanently at a measured force and then requires increasing force to stretch further. Manufacturers could also explore shaping it through permanent deformation, reducing dependence on machining.
why: Structural ceramics commonly break as cracks spread before they can stretch permanently. Controlled stretching would give designers a new mechanical behavior to account for alongside strength and fracture limits.

sources.who: Alexander Frisch, Xufei Fang and collaborators
sources.showed: Their review identifies 44 ceramic compounds with reported room-temperature deformation through dislocation motion in single crystals. It explains why deformation in tiny tests may fail to carry over to larger pieces.
sources.quote:
Second, we provide a materials toolbox listing 44 ceramic compounds that have been reported to exhibit 
dislocation plasticity at meso-/macroscale under ambient conditions.
sources.cited_for: Dislocations can carry permanent deformation in ceramics at room temperature.
sources.not_established: These reports do not establish sustained stretching under tension in a bulk, heat-resistant ceramic made of many grains.

sources.who: Xufei Fang, Wenjun Lu and collaborators
sources.showed: Adding mobile dislocations helped tiny strontium titanate single crystals deform under compression. The smallest pillars reached about 32% permanent strain without cracking.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate that this approach 
effectively suppresses crack formation and significantly promotes dislocation plasticity across the 
length scales, ranging from nanoscale to bulk testing.
sources.cited_for: Providing mobile dislocations can help ceramic crystals deform before they fracture.
sources.not_established: Compression of single crystals does not establish stable stretching across interacting grains in a structural-sized ceramic.

sources.who: Zhitong Xu, Jie Zhang, Liran Dong and collaborators
sources.showed: Their review describes room-temperature ceramic deformation through several mechanisms and identifies reliable deformation in bulk ceramics as a continuing challenge.
sources.quote: Recent studies have shown that ceramics exhibit RT plasticity through mechanisms including dislocation, phase transformation, and grain boundary sliding (GBS).
sources.cited_for: Ceramics have several routes to permanent deformation, but reliable bulk behavior remains difficult.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish the specific combination of bulk tensile stretching, interacting grains and heat-resistant material.

shown: Fang and collaborators reported about 32% permanent compression without cracking in tiny strontium titanate single crystals with added dislocations. Larger microscopic pillars also showed permanent deformation and required increasing stress as they deformed.

Room-temperature stretching has been reported in silver chloride made of many grains. That soft ceramic falls outside the heat-resistant structural target. The central step is sustained stretching in a bulk material whose neighboring grains must deform together.
missing: A bulk, heat-resistant ceramic must stretch permanently under tension at room temperature, harden as it stretches and stay intact.
Neighboring grains must accommodate each other's deformation without cracks ending the stretching.
Measurements must distinguish permanent stretching from elastic recovery, equipment movement and cracking, with repeatable results across batches.
Separate fracture and service tests must establish any claims about resisting damage or making useful components.

milestones.label: Bulk ceramic stretches permanently and hardens under tension
milestones.explanation: A representative heat-resistant ceramic made of many grains would have to yield, stretch uniformly and harden through dislocation motion at room temperature while staying intact. This would establish the central capability.

milestones.label: Measured stretching repeats across manufacturing batches
milestones.explanation: Reported methods, corrected strain measurements and microscopic evidence would have to confirm repeatable dislocation-driven stretching across specimens and batches. This would establish that the measured behavior is real.

milestones.label: Limits across sizes and grain structures are established
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish stretching, strength, hardening and failure limits across specimen sizes and grain structures. This would define the conditions under which the capability works.

milestones.label: Damage resistance and application claims pass separate tests
milestones.explanation: Fracture tests and relevant environmental, thermal, manufacturing and service tests would have to support claims about damage resistance or component use. This would establish benefits beyond permanent stretching.

uncertain: The route that lets neighboring grains stretch together before fracture remains unresolved for the target ceramic family.
Permanent stretching may not improve resistance to crack initiation or growth.
Application-specific specimen sizes, grain structures, repeatability requirements and acceptable measurement uncertainty remain to be defined.

page.title: Room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk ceramic polycrystals
page.definition: A bulk oxide, nitride or carbide made of many crystal grains undergoes permanent elongation under room-temperature tension, with a measurable reduction in cross-section at fracture. The strain is carried by dislocations, line defects that move through the crystal lattice.

goal.need: A 2026 review describes tensile fracture strengths of brittle ceramics as about one tenth to one fifteenth of their compressive fracture strengths. Compression therefore leaves their more fracture-sensitive loading mode untested. A 2025 survey catalogued 44 ceramic compounds with ambient-temperature dislocation plasticity, all with single-crystal demonstrations. The goal extends permanent deformation to bulk polycrystals under tension.

statements.body: MECERDIS, an ERC-funded research programme coordinated by Karlsruhe Institute of Technology
statements.quote: Beyond Project MECERDIS, many research facets centering around "room-temperature plastically deformable ceramics at bulk scale" shall be explored.
statements.context: The programme concerns dislocation engineering in functional ceramics; this statement identifies a bulk-plasticity research goal without specifying a tensile acceptance threshold.

statements.quote: This is why TU materials scientist Dr Xufei Fang is researching a new generation of ceramics that possess plastic ductility
statements.context: The university describes the research underlying the MECERDIS project.

completion.title: A bulk ceramic polycrystal shows permanent tensile deformation and reduced cross-section at fracture.
completion.criterion: A bulk polycrystalline oxide, nitride or carbide exhibits dislocation-mediated permanent deformation under room-temperature uniaxial tension and a measurable decrease in cross-sectional area at fracture. Bulk denotes macroscopic specimens, typically millimetre-sized or larger in the cited literature. The working rule prescribes no minimum percentage elongation or work-hardening rate.
completion.set_by: The ductility working rule of Sprackling, explicitly adopted for ceramics by Fang in Section 2 of his 2026 review; bulk tensile validation is separately identified by Frisch et al. in Section 2.6.
completion.threshold_quote: a sample deformed in tension as showing ductility if there is a measurable decrease in cross-section at fracture.
completion.basis: The working rule tests tensile ductility directly. Frisch et al. identify bulk tension as the decisive validation, while the bulk-scale definition distinguishes macroscopic specimens from local tests. The review published on 4 September 2026 still identifies bulk plasticity as challenging; its accessible abstract does not establish this narrower capability.

milestones.title: A ceramic crystal reaches 0.2% offset yield before fracture in room-temperature pillar compression.
milestones.criterion: Room-temperature pillar compression produces dislocation-mediated plastic flow beyond a 0.2% offset yield point. Fang et al.'s preprint reports about 430 MPa yield stress in seeded SrTiO3 pillars approximately 4 µm in diameter and 8 µm high. Two illustrated seeded pillars were stopped before fracture at approximately 8% and 25% plastic strain. The text describes additional reproducibility tests without giving their total specimen count.
milestones.set_by: The 0.2% offset yield convention, applied in Fang et al.'s SrTiO3 compression experiments and Supplementary Figure S5B; Fang's 2026 review also explicitly describes this convention for ceramic compression.
milestones.threshold_quote: yield strength of ~430 MPa (indicated using the 0.2% strain offset, see Supplementary Fig. S5B).

milestones.title: A ceramic polycrystal forms a dislocation-plastic surface zone without macroscopic cracking.
milestones.criterion: Room-temperature cyclic spherical indentation produces dislocation-mediated permanent surface deformation without macroscopic surface cracking. Okafor et al. demonstrated this in SrTiO3 with approximately 50 µm grains: a 2.5 mm ball under 1.5 kgf produced a plastic zone approximately 120 µm in diameter. They tested 1 and 10 indentation cycles, with at least 10 indents per testing condition on each sample. These dimensions describe the demonstration, not universal acceptance limits.
milestones.set_by: Cyclic Brinell indentation as used by Okafor et al., Sections 2.2 and 5, and recognised in Frisch et al.'s deformation toolbox. The published specimen conditions concern SrTiO3.
milestones.threshold_quote: was successfully generated via room-temperature cyclic indentation without macroscopic surface cracking.

milestones.title: A bulk ceramic polycrystal undergoes dislocation-mediated compression before brittle fracture.
milestones.criterion: A macroscopic oxide, nitride or carbide polycrystal exhibits dislocation-mediated plastic deformation before brittle fracture in room-temperature uniaxial compression. Słodczyk et al. use this experimental condition to classify bulk plasticity and describe bulk specimens as typically millimetre-sized or larger. Their criterion sets no minimum plastic strain. The cited 2025 review documents bulk-compression validation for single-crystal SrTiO3, KNbO3 and KTaO3; those results do not establish this polycrystalline stage.
milestones.set_by: The experimental bulk-plasticity classification published by Słodczyk et al., Section 2.2.1, consistent with the bulk-compression validation method described by Frisch et al., Section 2.5. Applied here to polycrystalline specimens.
milestones.threshold_quote: dislocation-mediated plastic deformation was shown to precede brittle fracture in bulk-scale uniaxial compression experiments conducted at room temperature.

not_found: Searches of ceramic tensile standards, roadmaps, programme objectives and prize criteria found no universal minimum elongation, hardening rate or specimen dimensions for this capability.
No report satisfying the complete bulk-polycrystalline oxide, nitride or carbide tensile criterion was located in searches through 14 November 2026.
The ASTM C1273 publisher page could not be opened; the accessible ISO 15490 preview specified tensile-strength testing without a ductility acceptance threshold.
Only the abstract of Xu et al.'s review published on 4 September 2026 was accessible.
The accessible seeded-SrTiO3 full text was the preprint; the publisher's journal full text could not be opened.
